findings.title: Allocators hand out a bare ndarray whose .ctypes.data is a dangling-pointer footgun if the array is not bound to a live name
findings.description: Every allocator returns a plain owned numpy.int64 array (allocate_buffer, duckdb_utils.py:7, via create_duckdb_* at lines 13/19/25/31/37/43/49). The buffer's lifetime is entirely caller-managed and there is no coupling between the buffer object and the handle/struct DuckDB writes into it. The whole out-param protocol depends on the caller keeping the *array* alive (not just the extracted handle int) for as long as DuckDB needs that memory: for single-handle buffers, until the matching duckdb_destroy_*(buf.ctypes.data); for the 48-byte duckdb_result buffer (create_duckdb_result, line 37), until duckdb_destroy_result reads internal_data out of the live struct. Because the allocator yields a bare ndarray, the idiomatic numpy footgun `p = create_duckdb_result().ctypes.data` (take .ctypes.data of an unbound temporary) leaves `p` dangling the instant the temporary is collected, and DuckDB's subsequent execute/destroy writes/reads freed heap. This is a real property of the API; it is not currently triggered -- every caller binds the array to a named local first (e.g. online_scoring.py:153,160-161 keeps `stmt` alive across the JIT loop and only extracts the handle int int(stmt[0]); test_ducklib.py:124-149 keeps `out_result` alive until duckdb_destroy_result). So this is a latent hazard the buffer API invites, not a present defect.
findings.impact: If any future caller (or example/doc copied by a user) writes the natural-looking `create_duckdb_result().ctypes.data` / `create_duckdb_*().ctypes.data` one-liner, the array is GC'd immediately and DuckDB writes the result struct (or a handle) into freed memory -- heap corruption / use-after-free, silent and intermittent. The 48-byte result buffer is the highest-stakes case because DuckDB stores the whole struct there and destroy dereferences it.
findings.recommendation: Document on the allocators that the returned array must outlive all DuckDB use of its .ctypes.data (the buffer, not the extracted handle int, is what must stay alive), or have callers/helpers take the buffer and its pointer in two steps. No code change is strictly required since no caller is currently affected; treat as an API-safety note.

notes: Reviewed /home/erik/projects/numbduck/numbduck/duckdb_utils.py in full plus the lifetime-sensitive consumers (examples/online_scoring.py:106-162, test/test_ducklib.py:997-1131, and the destroy idioms across test_ducklib.py / examples). Conclusion: the buffers themselves are memory-safe. They are owned numpy arrays (NRT-refcounted inside @njit, boxed to owned ndarrays when returned to Python); numpy never relocates a data buffer, so .ctypes.data is stable for the array's lifetime and there is no move/GC hazard originating in this file. Buffer sizes are correct: single-handle structs are one pointer (1xint64=8B) and duckdb_result is 48B (6xint64), matching duckdb.h v1.3.2 (duckdb_result = 6 pointer/idx_t fields) and the duckdb_result_ty=UniTuple(intp,6) used by the bindings -- no out-param OOB write. The handle-vs-buffer distinction holds: for single-handle buffers DuckDB only writes a pointer to its own memory into the buffer, so GC of the buffer after the handle int is extracted is harmless; only the matching duckdb_destroy_* (pointer-to-handle) needs the buffer alive again, which all callers honor. This file performs no meminfo/incref/decref, no ctypes.from_address reads, and no handle frees, so the MEM concerns in scope for that dimension (incref/decref balance, double-free of duckdb handles, raw from_address of GC-able objects, NRT leaks across raising calls) live in pybridge.py / the structref UDAF bridge (numbox meminfo) / the example destroy sequences, not here. The only thing attributable to duckdb_utils.py is the latent bare-ndarray .ctypes.data footgun captured as DBU-MEM-1 (low/low, no current caller triggers it). int64 (signed) storage of unsigned pointers is bit-preserving and not a memory issue.
